query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermomechanical treatment that promotes the in situ precipitation of fine, coherent intermetallic particles along the fcc/B2 lamellar interfaces in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy will enhance its yield strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance for fastener applications under extreme conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a uniform fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure whose intrinsic strength and plasticity are below industrial requirements.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored thermo-mechanical processing route – for example, a modest cold rolling reduction (around 8%) followed by an annealing treatment in the range of 600–700°C for a calibrated duration – to induce the controlled formation of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates at the lamellar phase boundaries.
generation.conditions: Processing conducted at room temperature (cold rolling) and subsequent annealing at 600–700°C (in an inert or controlled atmosphere to minimize oxidation) to promote fine precipitate formation. Subsequent mechanical testing should simulate service conditions including extreme temperature fluctuations (up to ~700°C), long-term static mechanical loading (creep tests at room temperature), and exposure to corrosive environments such as a 3.5% NaCl solution.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly dispersed, fine intermetallic precipitates located at the fcc/B2 lamellar interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates serve as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, thereby enhancing resistance to creep and mechanical deformation under long-term loading. In addition, a stabilized, refined lamellar architecture minimizes local galvanic differences, improving corrosion resistance. This combined precipitation strengthening and microstructural stabilization strategy is expected to elevate both strength and ductility simultaneously.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as‐cast baseline, the treated alloy is predicted to show a measurable improvement in yield and tensile strength, a higher ductility (improved plasticity), reduced room‐temperature creep strain rates, and a lower corrosion current density under aggressive conditions.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, characterized by its uniform lamellar structure but sub‐optimal strength, ductility, and resistance to creep and corrosion as required for fastener applications.
generation.boundary: The performance improvement should be realized under service conditions typical for fasteners: exposure to frequent and rapid temperature fluctuations (up to approximately 700°C), prolonged mechanical loading at ambient conditions, and corrosive environments such as saline solutions. The processing window (e.g., annealing temperature/time) must be tightly controlled to avoid precipitate coarsening or loss of ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The precise treatment parameters (annealing temperature, duration, and cold rolling reduction) require optimization; there is some uncertainty regarding the optimum precipitate chemistry and size to achieve the desired balance of enhanced mechanical and corrosion properties without compromising ductility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples. One set is processed by cold rolling with an ~8% reduction followed by annealing at 650°C for 30 minutes (in an inert atmosphere) to induce precipitate formation, while the control samples are maintained in the as-cast state. Subject both sets to standardized tensile tests, extended room-temperature creep tests (e.g., over 1000 hours), and corrosion tests in a 3.5% NaCl solution. Perform detailed microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM) to confirm the presence and distribution of precipitates.
measurements: Creep strain rate and creep rupture data
Corrosion current density and potential from electrochemical tests
Microstructural analysis (particle size, distribution, and phase identification)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the thermomechanically treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (for example, less than a 10% increase in tensile properties, no meaningful reduction in creep strain rate, or no improvement in corrosion resistance relative to the control) or if the intended nanoscale precipitates cannot be consistently identified in the microstructure.

cited_evidence.text: FeCrNi medium entropy alloy (MEA) has been widely regarded for its excellent mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. However, insufficient strength limits its industrial application. Intermetallic particle dispersion strengthening is considered to be an effective method to improve strength, which is expected to solve this problem. In this work, microstructural evolution and mechanical behavior of FeCrNi MEA with different Si content were investigated. We found that the precipitation of fine σ particles can be formed in situ by thermomechanical treatment of Si doping FeCrNi MEAs. The FeCrNiSi0.15 MEA exhibits a good combination of strength and ductility, with yield strength and tensile elongation of 1050 MPa and 7.84%, respectively. The yield strength is almost five times that of the as-cast FeCrNi MEA. The strength enhancement is mainly attributed to the grain-boundary strengthening and precipitation strengthening caused by fine σ particles.

The high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a single FCC structure has high ductility but low hardness. Although HEA with a single BCC structure has high strength and hardness, it also has low ductility. The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition.
